doc.title: Larry Gold interviewed by Monk Rowe, via Zoom, June 18, 2025

title: Tape reels and early overdubbing
summary: Gold describes big tape reels and how overdubbing meant bouncing between tape recorders in the early 1960s.

story.theme_name: In the studio: making records, then and now
story.community_name: Making records: studios, takes and the technology

blocks.x: Okay. This is my other prop, speaking of 1983.

That's a big reel too. Usually they weren't quite that big. That's almost double the amount of tape. Usually they were half that size but that wide. Yeah I mean, hey look, those days were special in lots and lots of different ways because a lot of that stuff was just being invented in a way too. It went from everyone recording live when I was a little boy in like '63 or '62. You used to have to go to another tape recorder to overdub. You would take what you had recorded on one tape recorder and do the orchestration to another tape
recorder, and maybe do that for the vocals and then all of a sudden your finished record had a couple generations worth of moving from one tape recorder to another.
Like The Beatles did. And this was prior to them doing that.
